stem: A 65-year-old man comes to the office due to a nonhealing ulcer on his right foot.  His medical history is significant for recurrent high blood glucose readings for the last several years, because he has not been taking his prescribed medications.  BMI is 37 kg/m2.  Physical examination is significant for a bilateral symmetric decrease in vibration sensation over the feet and ankles.  Which of the following is most likely to be associated with this patient's condition?​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌

options.label: D
options.text: Strong linkage with HLA class II gene makeup

options.label: E
options.text: Episodic ketoacidosis that requires insulin therapy

explanation:
The patient likely has type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM; advanced age, obesity, prolonged nonadherence with treatment without immediate life-threatening consequences).

The 2 cardinal defects involved in the pathophysiology of T2DM are increased insulin resistance and defective insulin secretion.  Early in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes, glucose tolerance is thought to remain normal because of a compensatory increase in insulin secretion from beta cells.  This compensatory insulin response by beta cells ultimately fails, causing poor glucose tolerance.

Thousands of genes likely contribute to T2DM development in association with environmental factors. A number of genetic and acquired factors are implicated in the beta-cell dysregulation of T2DM.  Islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin) is one factor thought to be responsible for this beta cell dysfunction.  Amylin is stored in insulin secretory granules and is co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells.  Deposits of amylin are universally seen in the pancreatic islets of patients with T2DM.  Amylin may play a role in beta cell apoptosis and defective insulin secretion.  

(Choices A, C, D and E)  These are features of type 1 diabetes mellitus (type 1 DM).  T1DM occurs when an autoimmune response is triggered by an environmental insult in genetically susceptible individuals.  Patients with T2DM retain at least some beta cell function, but patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus develop absolute deficiency of insulin secondary to immune destruction of pancreatic beta cells (insulinitis, islet cell antibodies).  These patients need insulin for survival, and discontinuation of insulin treatment results in ketoacidosis (which is much less likely in T2DM, although it can occur).  Certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class II genes (eg, HLA-DR and HLA-DQ haplotypes) are associated with a higher risk (eg, ~40%-50%) of T1DM.  However, the presence of these genetic haplotypes is not deterministic (ie, only ~5% of individuals with these haplotypes develop T1DM), and most cases of T1DM occur sporadically without a family history.

Educational objective:Pancreatic islet amyloid deposition is characteristic of type 2 diabetes mellitus.  A strong linkage with HLA class II gene makeup, pancreatic islet infiltration with leukocytes (insulitis), and antibodies against islet antigens are frequently seen in type 1 diabetes mellitus.​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌
